coherence.reasons: Both run the same clean hierarchy (why the US, which route, why not retail, how to make Amazon work) and each summary point maps to a section with matching numbers. X is slightly tighter, with four summary points that map one-to-one to sections. But its slide 8 title says only Amazon-led stays within the cash, payback and margin limits, while its own table shows Japan inside all three. It also plans on 28% ACoS and a 25% duty with a 29% gate, though its own break-even at 25% duty is 26.9%. Y words the same point more carefully ('the only route that builds a US business within the limits'). Its weakness is several ACoS thresholds (28% target, 30% review, 32% stop, 'plan on 30–32%') that sit above the 28.6% break-even, though it says openly that payback is then at risk. The flaws roughly offset.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred conclusion: Amazon-led with gates, retail deferred until awareness reaches 20%, and the $40M ambition reset. Both compare the options on the board's cap, payback and margin floor. Y weighs the trade-offs more fully. It says Japan is the only option that pays back in every modeled case and is the better choice if the board ranks payback certainty above the US ambition. It lists what would change its view, adds a repeat-rate checkpoint and a cumulative-cash stop of −$4M, and proposes a door test to measure the halo rather than assume it. It also asks the board to confirm how to read 'on the way to $40M'. X's single 29% ACoS gate is closer to the payback break-even than Y's 32% stop trigger, which is a real point for X. But X dismisses Japan mainly on size, has no repeat or volume condition, and gives no stop rule beyond 'hold spend'. Y's looser trigger is partly offset by its 28% target, 30% first-year review and cash stop.

evidence.reasons: The numbers in both match the key: $10.72/$4.00 Amazon contribution, $7.55 retail, B peak $20.8M and 4.5% margin, A at +$2.4M / +$0.4M / −$2.3M, break-even 28.6%, and $24.3M for B without the halo. Both test the 4.5 units per door and 25% ACoS against the benchmarks, reject the correlation as proof of a halo, set aside the $5.2B figure and note that two of three Amazon-first brands stalled. Y uses the evidence a little more fully. It notes pilot growth slowing from 16–17% to about 9% a month, runs volume sensitivities (−20% volume, break-even 27.0% at −10%) and a severe case, and shows 4,250 doors would be needed to cover retail fixed cost. It also splits B's revenue lead into halo and retail and states its evidence limits. Y has minor overstatements: 'most' is bought on Amazon at 41%, Saebom reached '$30M on Amazon' when the pack gives total US revenue, and a 2031–32 extrapolation, labeled illustrative. X's slips are the 'only route within limits' title contradicted by its Japan row, 'rebuy as often as peers' at 29% against 31%, and no volume sensitivity.

revision.reasons: Both handle the CEO's hypothesis as the key expects: keep the Amazon-first route and add conditions. Both replace the 25% ACoS assumption, raise the retail awareness trigger from 15% to 20% using the 3.5 median against the 4.0 delisting line, add the label and entity fix, and reset the 2030 ambition to about $26M. X sets this out as an explicit before-and-after of five settings, including the tariff, and puts its ACoS gate near the break-even. Y adds a door test before any rollout, a stop trigger and a repeat checkpoint, but its ACoS thresholds are looser. Neither over- nor under-revises, and the difference is negligible.

overall.reasons: The two documents reach the same defensible recommendation from essentially the same correct model, so the gap is small. Y serves the board somewhat better. It turns the analysis into five explicit decisions, with a funded $4M envelope, staged checkpoints and stop triggers. It states the Japan trade-off honestly and the conditions under which the recommendation would change, and it tests volume risk and pilot deceleration as well as ACoS and tariff. X is tighter and its ACoS gate fits the payback constraint better. But it overstates that only Amazon-led is within the limits, underweights Japan as a real alternative, and offers fewer conditions and triggers.
